name: M.27

origin.note: Cross made 1929 and selected 1934 (trialled as Malling 3431); not released to growers until the mid-1970s.

support: Permanent stake or wires for life
soil_notes: Only for deep, fertile, well-drained soil kept free of grass and weeds; needs regular watering and feeding or trees stall ('runt out').
best_for: very small gardens, stepovers, mini-cordons, dwarf pyramids and large containers
avoid_when: poor, dry, wet or grassed ground; replant sites; weak or spur-type varieties; severe-winter regions
variety_fit: Best with vigorous varieties (including triploids) that would be too big on M.9; weak growers and spur types make tiny, stunted trees.
notes: The most dwarfing of the Malling stocks, giving a tree roughly half the size of one on M.9 that crops in its second or third year. Roots are small and brittle, so the tree needs a stake for life and good growing conditions. Collar rot resistance is good, but it is susceptible to woolly aphid; fire blight ratings vary between sources (Ontario lists it as tolerant, US extension as highly susceptible).

name: M.9

origin.parentage: selected from the French 'Jaune de Metz' paradise stock (found c. 1879)
origin.note: One of the old paradise types sorted and numbered at East Malling from 1912; virus-cleaned EMLA and continental clones replaced the original from the 1970s.

support: Permanent stake or trellis for life
soil_notes: Needs fertile, well-drained soil with a weed-free strip; irrigate in dry spells; shallow brittle roots tolerate collar rot but not drought or competition.
best_for: small gardens, cordons, espaliers, spindles and intensive orchards on good soil
avoid_when: poor, dry or grassed ground; fire-blight areas; cold-winter zones 4 and below; exposed sites without support
variety_fit: Pairs well with vigorous, triploid and tip-bearing varieties; weak growers and spur types can end up under-sized.
notes: The world's reference dwarfing stock: very precocious and efficient, with good fruit size, but brittle roots mean the tree must be supported for life. It is very susceptible to fire blight (whole-tree loss through rootstock blight) and woolly aphid, forms burr knots on exposed shank, and roots are injured in severe winters. Clones differ in vigour: Pajam 2 and Nic29 are the strongest, T337 and Fleuren 56 the weakest; virus-free EMLA 9 is a little larger than the original virus-infected M.9.

name: Pajam 1

origin.parentage: clonal selection of M.9 ('Paradis Jaune de Metz') from French stoolbeds
origin.note: Selection programme begun in 1974 by CTIFL with INRA and nurseries; US plant patent PP7714 (filed 1989, granted 1991). Sister clone Pajam 2 (Cepiland) is the more vigorous one.

support: Permanent stake or trellis for life
soil_notes: As for M.9: fertile, well-drained, weed-free soil with irrigation in dry spells.
best_for: high-density spindle and super-spindle orchards; trained garden forms on good soil
avoid_when: poor, dry or grassed ground; fire-blight areas; severe-winter regions
variety_fit: Behaves like a mid-vigour M.9; suits moderately vigorous varieties in intensive systems, while weak varieties are better on Pajam 2 or Nic29.
notes: A French virus-free M.9 clone that roots more easily in the stoolbed than older M.9 lines. In trials it sits in the middle of the M.9 clones for vigour: a little stronger than T337 and EMLA 9 in NC-140 work, weaker than Pajam 2 and Nic29, and similar to standard M.9 in some European trials. It keeps all of M.9's weaknesses (brittle roots, fire blight, woolly aphid) and can sucker noticeably.

name: M.8

origin.parentage: old French paradise stock, recorded before 1696
origin.note: Numbered in the East Malling sorting of paradise stocks; the American 'Clark Dwarf' interstem was later identified as M.8.

soil_notes: Weak, brittle-rooted stock needing good, sheltered soil; rarely used on its own roots.
best_for: historical and breeding interest; formerly a dwarfing interstem on hardy seedling roots
avoid_when: any cold or exposed site; commercial or low-maintenance planting
notes: An old dwarfing paradise stock, rated among the least winter-hardy of the original Malling types, with brittle wood and roots. In North America it was sold as the 'Clark Dwarf' interstem between a hardy seedling root and the variety, giving small trees that tended to lean and break at the unions. Its main legacy is as a parent of Budagovsky B.9 (M.8 x 'Red Standard').

name: M.26
support: Stake advised for life on light, exposed or windy sites; may stand alone on deep good soil
soil_notes: Wants well-drained loam; very intolerant of wet feet; plant with the union only 2-5 cm above soil to limit burr knots on the exposed shank.
best_for: small to medium gardens, bush and spindle trees, and large containers on reasonable soil
avoid_when: poorly drained or heavy wet soils; fire-blight regions; very cold zones without hardier alternatives
variety_fit: Graft incompatibility has been reported with some cultivars (e.g. 'Rome Beauty' and 'Stayman'); in the UK Cox on M.26 is noted as prone to collar rot.
notes: A dwarfing-to-semi-dwarf stock between M.9 and M.7 in size, precocious and productive, and stronger rooted than M.9 though still best staked. It is very susceptible to fire blight and burr knots, and its collar rot rating depends on region (resistant in UK trials, susceptible in North America). Older US guides called it the hardiest M/MM stock, but root injury in severe test winters means it is not a substitute for Budagovsky or Geneva stocks in cold zones.

name: M.7

origin.parentage: old Doucin-type stock of unknown parentage, probably of French origin
origin.note: Sorted from the mixed paradise/doucin stocks at East Malling from 1912; virus-free EMLA 7 is noticeably more vigorous than old infected M.7.

support: Stake for the first years; may lean under heavy crops or on shallow, windy sites
soil_notes: Widely adapted to most well-drained to moderately drained soils; avoid heavy clay and very shallow soil.
best_for: semi-dwarf free-standing or lightly supported trees in gardens and older-style orchards
avoid_when: heavy clay; sites where suckers would be a nuisance (lawns, mown orchards)
variety_fit: Compatible with most varieties; some US guides advise against it for 'Delicious' types because of leaning.
notes: A long-established semi-dwarf stock, fairly tolerant of fire blight and collar rot and adaptable to many soils, but it suckers heavily and is only moderately precocious. Shallow roots can let trees lean, so early staking helps. Hardiness is moderate: the roots are tender and benefit from snow cover or mulch in hard winters.

name: MM.106

origin.place: East Malling Research Station and John Innes Institute, Merton
origin.parentage: Northern Spy x M.1 (some US sources give M.2)
origin.note: Bred in the joint East Malling / John Innes programme for woolly aphid resistance; introduced 1952.

support: Stake for 3-5 years; free-standing after that except on exposed sites
soil_notes: Copes with lighter, poorer and grassed soils but must be well drained; very prone to Phytophthora collar rot in wet or heavy ground.
best_for: general garden and orchard trees: bush, half-standard, espalier and fans on most well-drained soils
avoid_when: waterlogged or heavy clay soils; frost-pocket sites prone to sharp early-winter freezes
variety_fit: Widely compatible and good for weak or spur-type varieties; in the UK Cox on MM.106 is especially exposed to collar rot. Very susceptible to tomato ringspot virus.
notes: The UK's most popular all-round apple stock: well anchored, almost sucker-free, precocious and tolerant of poorer soils and drought. Its weaknesses are severe collar rot on badly drained soils and slow autumn hardening, which leaves trees exposed to early-winter freezes even though fully dormant trees are reasonably hardy. Woolly aphid resistance from Northern Spy is good but has broken down locally where resistant-breaking aphid strains occur.

name: MM.111

origin.place: East Malling Research Station and John Innes Institute, Merton
origin.note: Merton 793 is itself Northern Spy x M.2; introduced 1952.

support: Free-standing; stake only for the first 2-3 years if planted as an older tree
soil_notes: Adapted to most soils and the most drought-tolerant Malling-Merton stock; dislikes waterlogging. Light soils keep trees smaller.
best_for: half-standards, standards and large free-standing trees; light, dry or poor soils; base stock for interstem trees
avoid_when: small gardens; waterlogged soils; when fast cropping is needed
variety_fit: Good for weak growers and spur types; vigorous upright varieties make large trees.
notes: A vigorous, deep-rooted, well-anchored stock that tolerates drought, poorer soils and grass competition, with good woolly aphid resistance and fair tolerance of fire blight and collar rot on drained ground. It is slow to come into full bearing (often 6-7 years) and forms burr knots on exposed shank. Fairly winter hardy and widely used in colder North American orchards.
